[ 2 ] [ 3 ] Description [ edit ] Wild Mountain Cafe operates from a purple house in Seattle . It has a front garden and porch, [ 4 ] and serves American cuisine . The menu has included Eggs Benedict , [ 5 ] French toast , fried chicken , [ 4 ] granola , huevos rancheros , macaroni and cheese , potato pancakes , and a version of chicken Parmesan with bread crumbs . [ 6 ] [ 7 ] The drink menu has included Bloody Marys and mimosas . [ 5 ] History [ edit ] Desirae Aylesworth has been the owner since 2019. [ 8 ] [ 9 ] [ 10 ] She runs the cafe with her husband and a small staff. [ 11 ] Previously, the business was owned by Roo McKenna and Connie Stone, [ 12 ] who opened Wild Mountain Cafe in 2002. [ 13 ] Someone broke into the restaurant in 2009. [ 14 ] Reception [ edit ] The Not for Tourists Guide to Seattle has said the cafe offers "tasty, funky, spirited home-grown food". [ 15 ] Wild Mountain has been highlighted as one of the Seattle metropolitan area 's best woman-owned eateries. [ 5 ] [ 16 ] References [ edit ] ↑ Kasinger, Chona (September 8, 2016). raw_text: The Source Family By Dimitri Ehrlich May 13, 2013 View Full Images We really did live in another dimension of reality. We had our own protocols. We always said that we were living by spiritual law over man’s law. Isis Aquarian In the late 1960s, my parents bought a pre-Civil War farmhouse near Woodstock, New York, and for many years my family spent summers there. It wasn’t an official commune, but several other families moved in with us for varying periods of time. We all did yoga and ate health food, learned about meditation, and generally acted like hippies. My parents were devotees of various teachers and gurus, including Baba Ram Dass, Chögyam Trungpa, Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, and Alan Watts, and my brother and sister and I were raised in a world where Buddhism and Taoism were part of the daily macrobiotic stew. As the dissention bred by the war in Vietnam, the upending of traditional power structures spurred by the civil rights and sexual liberation movements, and the numerous other cultural revolutions of the era began to take hold, many young people started to seek ways of applying the spirit of those social transformations to exploring their own consciousness. Some of them found religion—both in organized form and in the form of more esoteric branches and movements. Others joined communes that were interested in finding new ways of living and being. Still others joined what eventually turned out to be cults. Around the same time that I was enjoying my idyllic hippie childhood in the Catskill Mountains, thousands of communes were springing up across the country, most of them peaceful and innocuous, while others—like those led by Jim Jones and Charles Manson—more nefarious. Among the hundreds of self-styled guru figures dotting the American landscape in the late ’60s and early ’70s was a man named Jim Baker, a former Marine and World War II vet who had rechristened himself Father Yod, and who is now the subject of the new documentary The Source Family , directed by Jodi Wille and Maria Demopoulos. Baker had a less than savory past: in addition to having abandoned two marriages, he was also said to have been involved in a number of bank robberies and to have killed two men in separate incidents, apparently in self-defense. By the end of the ’60s, though, Baker had amassed considerable wealth. He’d opened Los Angeles’s pioneering health-food restaurant, the Source, on Sunset Strip, and was leading meditation classes. He’d also begun to attract a circle of attractive young men and women, many of whom would eventually become members of the Source Family, a commune led by Baker that mixed teachings from a variety of belief systems, ranging from theosophy and tantrism to kundalini and astrology. Baker’s restaurant became the epicenter of a cool new lifestyle and health-food consciousness: John Lennon, Steve McQueen, and Warren Beatty all ate there; Woody Allen shot a famous scene from Annie Hall (1977) there. The income from the restaurant also allowed the members of the Source Family to live much larger than most commune-dwellers: Baker was whisked around town in a white Rolls-Royce and rented a mansion with an Olympic-size swimming pool in Los Feliz, where he soon came to live with more than 100 Family members. The Source Family also had a rock band, Ya Ho Wa 13, which explored the fringes of psychedelic rock while Baker (somewhat haphazardly) banged on drums and chanted (vinyl pressings of Ya Ho Wa 13’s recordings have become obsessed-over collectors’ items). Baker was—to say the least—a complicated character. At one point, he had 14 “spiritual wives,” some of whom were teenagers. But while he undeniably demanded a certain dedication among his followers, he wasn’t a tyrannical leader, and Demopoulos and Wille’s documentary neither demonizes him nor shies away from his more controversial behavior. “My opinion of Father Yod is that he was not a charlatan,” says Wille, who spent six years interviewing more than 40 former Source Family members for the film. “He had charlatan aspects to him, but Father Yod fits squarely into what the scholar Robert Ellwood would call the ‘magus tradition.’ The magus is not a saint; he’s not even really a seer or a prophet, but he’s kind of an initiator. He serves as this figure who has more access to other realms than others. People like that existed in ancient Greece and throughout every culture, and they were always questioned by the authority. Father Yod, to me, has a lot less in common with Charles Manson than he does with Pythagoras.” Nevertheless, it was the fearful comparisons to the former rather than the latter that eventually drove Baker and the Source Family from their compound, which was located just blocks from where the LaBianca murders occurred. Eventually, in 1975, the entire Family moved to Hawaii, where they faced a hostile reception from the locals, as well as money troubles. After Baker fatally injured himself in a hang-gliding accident, his followers began to drift apart. The story of the Source Family might have been largely forgotten were it not for the 2007 book The Source: The Untold Story of Father Yod, Ya Ho Wa 13, and the Source Family , by Family members Isis Aquarian and Electricity Aquarian. Demopoulos and Wille’s documentary builds upon the work of the book, and we learn that, nearly 40 years on, some former Family members have become quite successful (one, Magus, founded a software-industry staffing company that eventually sold for $60 million), while others haven’t fared as well (Baker’s legal wife, Robin, is described by her daughter in the film as being broken by her experiences). But most of those interviewed don’t regret their time with the Family. “There were so many people in the Family who have gone on to do amazing things who claim that the Source Family was an important foundation for who they became,” Wille says. “It’s easy to look at these sorts of groups and just look at the psychology and what a mess they were, but they were social incubators for some of the brightest lights of the culture. They also destroyed some people or really screwed up some people for decades. Some people really had a hard time recovering from the Source in the years after it fell apart, and it took them years to get their shit together.” For her part, Wille sees Father Yod as a kind of Jungian archetype. “He was totally human,” she says. “He was heavily flawed, and some say he had narcissistic tendencies, but ultimately what he provided for Family members was enough to give them the opportunity to have a radical personal transformation. And I feel like these groups become, in some ways, the transformers of a culture.” I recently spoke by phone with Isis Aquarian and Electricity Aquarian, both of whom appear in the documentary and still live in Hawaii. DIMITRI EHRLICH: What were your respective childhoods like? ISIS: I was the oldest of seven children. We were in the military so we moved a lot. My mom was a saint—an absolutely loving, perfect mother. Took very good care of us. My dad was an alcoholic, which in the ’50s was just kind of what military men were. We were, to a degree, a dysfunctional family. First of all, we had way too many kids, and we were moving all the time, so it was hard. It basically led to all of us wanting to get out as soon as possible. ELECTRICITY: Very similar story in a lot of ways. I was born in Columbia, South Carolina. My dad was an alcoholic, my mother was a saint. She’s 93 years old now and still lives in the South. We had a pretty rough childhood. I had an older brother who absorbed most of the violence and difficulty, so that enabled me to retain some of my innocence. But, in general, it was a standard Southern upbringing. I think probably most of the children I knew had alcoholic fathers at that time. EHRLICH: What religion were you? ISIS: I was pretty much raised Catholic. I never really remember buying into it. I loved the incense. When they walked down the aisle with the incense, I always remember thinking, Oh my god, that is so cool. People didn’t find Father. he basically magnetized us. He attracted to him those who had the vision to see him. Electricity Aquarian ELECTRICITY: I was raised in the Baptist church. I was pretty devout. I stood up on the pulpit in front of the church when I was 6 years old and told the entire congregation that I was going to be a preacher. That lasted until I was about 12 or 13, as late as 14, when I began to realize that it was too many lies. So I went to a lot of other different religions to check them out. By the time I was in college, I considered myself to be a pretty staunch atheist. EHRLICH: What was your first exposure to any kind of mystical experience or meditation? ISIS: Growing up I had psychic experiences where I knew I had guides, and I never really related it to a religion. When I got out of high school, I was searching for something but I just never could find anything that really grabbed me. I dropped out and came to L.A.—the hippie and flower-children thing was happening. It was like a portal opened and a whole society in certain pockets of America embraced a new type of spirituality of relating to each other and living. That’s what the ’60s and ’70s were about, without going into all of it: the food, the diet, the vegetarianism, everything. When I left my family, I got a job with my congressman and moved to D.C. and very quickly realized that I did not want to be that type of a socialite or marry that type of a person who lived that life. I was very drawn to the flower children and the hippie energy. ELECTRICITY: I graduated from the University of South Carolina in the summer of 1968. I was leaving and my wife wouldn’t go with me, so the day after I graduated, I put books and records and a few clothes in my VW Bug and left for San Francisco. I had bought some little plastic daisies and stuck them on my VW. [ laughs ] I was going looking for something better. I wanted something more. So I drove straight to San Francisco and rented a closet under the stairwell in a brownstone in Berkeley with all the students—graduate students mostly. Of course, they began to expand my mind right away. Within a couple of months, I moved into the city, right off of Haight. You did not live in the Haight-Ashbury district and stay conservative and ignorant of what was going on. Just to walk down the street with people standing on the street corners saying, “Grass and acid, grass and acid,” and the local hippie girls wearing overcoats so they could go out in the tourist cars and flash them for money . . . It was a really wild scene, and your mind just immediately began to grow dramatically—in spiritual ways as well as physical ways. But we began to seek out something better and go to meditate with the various yogis who would come to town and the gurus, and do our own meditations. I fell in love with this little lady, and we lived up on Potrero Hill, and we began to almost have our own little family, our own little commune. We had a group of people who were attracted to us and gathered around us. We would all meditate together and study various forms of spirit. But the first time my mind was completely blown way, way, way beyond what I had known before was when I met Father. That was in January of 1974. ISIS: When I dropped out of New York and went to L.A., we all went to the Old World Restaurant, and that was my first meeting with Jim Baker. He was married at the time to Dora, a French girl, and she and I became very good friends. I never really connected with Jim Baker at the time. I mean, he was fabulous. He was a Hollywood legend. He was being called a food guru because he had all these amazing, successful restaurants on Sunset. I became engaged to a very famous rock ‘n’ roll photographer [Ron Raffaelli], and we were working in the field and needed models for a poster campaign for Jesus Christ Superstar . I had heard that Jim Baker had opened up a new restaurant called the Source down on Sunset, and there were guys who had long hair and looked like Jesus. So I went down one day, stepped onto the patio, and out came a man looking like Moses. He was no longer the Jim Baker I knew. Something happened immediately. It was an absolute, immediate turnaround, and that was it—I knew I was home. I knew that was what I had been looking for. His frequency merged with mine and it uplifted me. I never looked back. ELECTRICITY: If you interviewed a hundred of the Family members, you would probably be blown away by the similarities of the stories that everybody will tell you. But I always say: people didn’t find Father, he basically magnetized us. He attracted to him those who had the vision to see him. I was living in San Francisco. I had picked up a kid named Scott hitchhiking one day and it turned out he was a phenomenal musician. I invited him to live with me for a while, while he worked on his music. We decided to go to Los Angeles, so we packed up my ’51 Chevy and spent a week pounding our heads against brick walls, getting nowhere, and many times going by this restaurant that had all these amazing people working there—men with white robes and long hair and beards, and beautiful women. We were fascinated by it, but we couldn’t afford to stop and eat, so we just kept looking at it. Finally, we were out of money, we were out of ideas, we had spent all day sitting in David Geffen’s parking place in his parking lot. He didn’t come to work that day, so we decided to go to Venice Beach and drop acid and see if we could come up with any ideas. Scott pulled out a leaflet and said, “Let’s go to this concert at the Venice Pavilion.” It was a concert being put on by the Source Family. After the show, Scott sat down to play one of his songs at the piano. Some of the sons got Father to listen to the song, and he talked to us and invited us to meditation the next morning. I knew from that point that my life had changed. ISIS: We really did live in another dimension of reality. We had our own protocols and we always said we were living by spiritual law over man’s law. I was pretty much focused on him. He was my thread. And then when he started having other women and stuff, that didn’t bother me. The women were sisters beforehand. To me, it worked. You talk to some of the other women, and you might hear a different story. But I did not have that karmic thread with him. In fact, I never felt like I had drama with him. We were there in agreement from before we even came into this life to do the work. EHRLICH: What was your first impression of Father Yod? ISIS: My first impression was absolutely knowing what I was doing with him and who he was. The Family was phenomenal. We had a phenomenal life. We were very wealthy, but money didn’t mean anything. We lived in a mansion. We drove Rolls-Royces. And we had fun and we had each other. We had morning meditations. I mean, we had everything. ELECTRICITY: The next morning after we met him, we went to meditations, and that was where my impressions were burned into my psyche forever. As you approached this amazing room with the most amazing smells coming from it, you heard this awesome chanting. You opened the door and there’s this incense-filled room with over a hundred people sitting in the lotus position in front of Father—just staggering power and beauty. We stood in the back of the room and he said, “You’re late!” We were late because we were driving slowly to make sure we didn’t run out of gas before we got there. [ laughs ] He said, “Would I be showing you more love if I allowed you to stay or if I made you leave?” He was looking right at me, and I learned later on that he was always looking right at everybody. So I said my preference would be that you allowed us to stay, and he said, “That’s exactly what I thought. Get out!” So my first impression . . . I went out storming. “Nobody is going to talk to me that way.” But I did come back the next morning. EHRLICH: What did your family and friends say when you entered the Source Family? ISIS: That’s what you did with the yogis and the gurus at the time, so it wasn’t a foreign concept. You left your old life, which included your family and friends. If they weren’t on that path with you, then they got left behind. I always stayed in touch with my mom, and she always knew where I was. But we did turn around and embrace a new life. And most of us did not look back during that time, because we had such a full, complete life. And most people did not come from a family situation where they had too much going for them to begin with. ELECTRICITY: Most of us—of our generation—were estranged from our families or relationships were strained our their families. So it was easy for us when Father said, basically, that the only way you can truly get on the path is to leave your past behind—your family and your friends. And if you don’t, then you need to bring them with you on the path—otherwise they’ll hold you back. So it was very painful for a lot of people, and we did have to go back later on and heal relationships. But in general, we walked away from our past, and that’s why we got new names. We even got new drivers’ licenses. But I would keep my mother apprised; I’d speak to her once every three to six months. EHRLICH: When you had 140 people living in a three-bathroom house, who bought the toilet paper? ISIS: Everybody had a duty. The women who stayed at home took care of the house perfectly. Everything was clean. There was food that was brought to the house. I don’t know how we lived with three bathrooms, but it worked. I never remember having to wait for the bathroom. But going to the bathroom when you are a vegetarian or on a very clean diet and lifestyle is a little different than going to the bathroom if you’re not—if you know what I mean. EHRLICH: What was the best aspect of Father Yod’s character and what was his worst flaw? ISIS: His best aspect was his ability to completely change in the moment and be open and present. From hitting what we called “the Earth trip” if somebody was having an issue, and going right back into spirit. He was a man’s man but he was also a woman’s man. He was very powerful. And his worst aspect probably was just being impatient at times, because, when you’re moving so fast with spirit through the universe and things aren’t manifesting as fast as you want them to on the Earth plane . . . With 200 people, it can get frustrating. EHRLICH: Given that he’d been involved in the deaths of two people and apparently robbed banks and abandoned wives and families, did you ever think, Maybe he shouldn’t be my guru? ISIS: For us, it was removed; it was that part of him in the past, and that’s not a part we knew. And it was his part to figure out on his life journey and amend or clean up. That was not our karmic thing to do with him; that was his. But he told us everything. He would spend morning after morning talking about killing the person, robbing the bank. It was like an oral history for the next generation. And he only spoke in the third person once he became Father Yod—Jim Baker became another entity for him. ELECTRICITY: He was no longer Jim Baker. Jim Baker died, Father Yod was born. So no karma came with him. ISIS: He always assumed the responsibility for anything he did or any harm he caused anybody when he was Jim Baker. And he took steps to go back and apologize or talk with them or pay people back money if he owed it to them. ELECTRICITY: He always said, “Learn from the past, keep an eye peeled on the future, but live in the now.” And that’s exactly how he lived his life. ISIS: He used to laugh at Jim Baker all the time. EHRLICH: Didn’t the fact that he was with 14 women at once contravene one of his Ten Commandments and— ELECTRICITY: Pardon me. No, it doesn’t contravene. It doesn’t say that man and one woman will be one. It says, “The man and his woman will be one.” That doesn’t mean necessarily that it will limit it to one woman. ISIS: He said, “I’m not going to have mistresses and keep them in the closet, like some yogis do. I’m going to be out front with what I’m doing, because I respect women.” EHRLICH: In the documentary, Electra says he was also commanding people to have sex with certain other people. ISIS: That totally blew my mind. I didn’t agree with what everybody was saying. That was not my reality. I never saw it come down that way, and I never saw anybody being unhappy about their choices. He always said that if you don’t want to be with somebody, you don’t have to. He asked many of the women to be with a Son, and they went, “Well, I really don’t want to,” so that was it. Maybe the blindly obedient would not feel the same. So that whole thing with Electra [a female member of the Family who appears in the documentary] about being with Mercury [a male member], it didn’t make sense to me. That was how she saw it for some reason. Did you see a picture of Mercury? Like, oh my god, you’re complaining about being with this person. [ all laugh ] Please, step aside. Let me at him. ELECTRICITY: Forty years later, some people have colored their memories by what they want to remember and what they need to remember in order to fit into their current lives or to try to fit back into the life they had before the Family. ISIS: I’m sure that with some people, some of it wasn’t good. It was good while we were together because we lived in our own reality. But when you step back into the Earth’s reality, you don’t fit. They were trying to make something fit from that frequency into this frequency, and it didn’t fit for them, so then they started becoming negative and judging it. That’s not the way I saw it, but if that was their perspective, then that’s true for them, and I allow it. I’m sure he wasn’t all that grand to everybody; I just never had an issue with it, so it’s hard for me to see that something was not right. But if it wasn’t right, why did everybody stay for years and put up with it. I just remember people laughing and being happy and saying, “My god, best time ever.” Anybody in the movie who wasn’t happy will turn around and go, “But I wouldn’t have changed it for anything.” ELECTRICITY: He’d always say, “If you are not happy, if you see anything wrong with what I say, please bring something better to me or let me know or leave.” So everybody who was there was absolutely there and absolutely committed. And as they look back on it and reinterpret things with their current perspectives, sometimes their memories seem to have changed. But we do allow them that, as Isis said. EHRLICH: I got the impression that he committed suicide at the end because— ISIS: I’m going to cut you off because I know what you’re after, if you don’t mind. He tried to disperse the Family several times. Once we left L.A., that was it. It just went downhill for us. It no longer worked. When we were in Kauai, he said, “Let’s disperse the Family.” The Family wouldn’t leave. He said, “It’s time for everybody to go out on their own—this isn’t working.” And he said, “I’ve given you everything I have, you don’t need anything else.” We wouldn’t go. So he didn’t commit suicide, but he wanted out, he was ready to go. He knew that he couldn’t leave the Family, and we weren’t going to leave him. So he tested it. He said, “I’m going to go off a cliff. I’m going to go hang gliding.” But I think he had a thought in the back of his mind: “Oh my god, please, if this could be an opportunity to take me, I’m so ready to go.” EHRLICH: So it wasn’t suicide— ISIS: When we found him, he had no broken bones, he wasn’t bleeding. He was conscious. He said he had a pain in his back. Nobody ever thought he was leaving the body. He said something like, “Well, I guess that’s my last lesson from god. I thought I was doing that, but I wasn’t.” He did leave the body. It’s what he wanted. And he had an M.O. from the time he was Jim Baker. I traced it back— ELECTRICITY: Isis! ISIS: Okay, well, he was done with it, and he walked, and he left. And that’s what he did with us. He just left. ELECTRICITY: We had a conversation recently on our private Family site, and no one ever suggested that he had committed suicide. He taught us that suicide was not part of the spiritual path. One of the Sons, who was a hang glider and who loaned him his kite, said, “Why would he have flown in a beautiful pattern and landed the kite if he were trying to commit suicide?” He actually had a good landing. It was a little bit of a hard landing, but I’ve had more scratches on my leg from cats than he had on his leg from the landing. So that’s the final statement: He landed the kite. The kite was not even damaged. You don’t commit suicide by landing a kite. You fly into the cliff or the ocean or whatever. EHRLICH: Where are each of you living now? ISIS: I live on the island of Oahu, Hawaii. ELECTRICITY: I live on Kauai, Hawaii. EHRLICH: And how are you both living? ISIS: Very well. [ laughs ] We are very lucky to be here. We both have nice homes. We both have work that we do. We have family around us. We travel. Electricity is my Source partner, and we have a lot of projects we’ve been working on. Sometimes I go to Kauai and sometimes he comes here. I’m 71 and retired. ELECTRICITY: I have several businesses. I have been a licensed real estate broker in the state of Hawaii for about 24 years, and in the last five years, I’ve been putting together a business called Soulgrowth.org, an online portal for all matters of spirit and an effort to draw everybody together on all spiritual paths and give them a place to come and become one. EHRLICH: Looking back now, what did you learn from the whole experience? ISIS: I have absolutely no fear of death. I understand karma in this life. I understand incarnation threads. I understand spirit. I would say I’m not a complete vegetarian, but I have the wisdom and I’ve retained that thread with him. It’s still an ongoing thing. It gives me new stuff everyday. ELECTRICITY: I do all of this work not only because I think this is a very good story, but also to inspire everyone to seek their own soul’s growth. Father always said, “We don’t need any middle men between us and god.” And he’d say, “Which path? It does not matter as long as you have the strength to stay on it.” So the best way we found to boil down his teachings is to use what he would always call our aim. I’ve renamed it the path of the PERL: Purify your body; Elevate your mind; Refine your emotions; Liberate your soul. Once you start on that path, you can do absolutely anything you want to do, as long as you’re kind. DIMITRI EHRLICH IS A CONTRIBUTING MUSIC EDITOR FOR INTERVIEW. He founded a spiritual commune in the Hollywood Hills known as The Source Family . He was also lead singer of the commune's experimental psychedelic rock band, Ya Ho Wha 13. Contents Sol ammon source family first born on family father yod Home father yod and the spirit of 76 Early life Source Family Music Death Legacy References Home father yod and the spirit of 76 Early life James Edward Baker was born on July 4, 1922, in Cincinnati, Ohio. Baker earned the Silver Star as a United States Marine in World War II and became expert in jujutsu . He moved to California to become a Hollywood stuntman and was influenced by the Nature Boys, a Los Angeles -based group of beats who lived a natural lifestyle, maintained vegetarian diets, and lived "according to Nature's Laws". Baker also studied philosophy, religion and esoteric spiritual teachings, even becoming a Vedantic monk for a time. He later became a follower of Yogi Bhajan , a Sikh spiritual leader and teacher of Kundalini Yoga. In 1969, Baker founded the Source Restaurant on Los Angeles's Sunset Strip . The restaurant served organic vegetarian food, with such celebrity regulars as John Lennon , Julie Christie and Marlon Brando . Jim Baker had two other successful restaurants on Sunset Strip: the Aware Inn and the Old World. Despite the claims that he had fourteen different wives, he had only one legal wife, Robin Popper, to whom he was married in 1970. They had a daughter together, Tau, born August 14, 1974. Robin said at the time he was "a dirty old man on a lust trip". Source Family Baker left Yogi Bhajan in the late 1960s and created his own philosophy based on Western mystery tradition . Changing his name to Father Yod and Ya Ho Wha, Baker became the patriarch of a commune of young people, who considered him their spiritual father. The group, known as The Source Family , lived together in a Hollywood Hills mansion and was supported by the earnings of the Source Restaurant, which grossed $10,000 a day during its peak popularity. Some of the doctrines of the Source Family were kept secret; however, they generally adopted a way of life that promoted natural health, organic vegetarian diets, communal living and utopian ideals. Father Yod/Ya Ho Wha had a core communal group of 150 people living in the Hollywood Hills. He had 14 wives and 3 children. Music Music was an integral part of the Source Family and many members were musicians. Father Yod formed an improvisational psychedelic rock band called Ya Ho Wha 13, with himself as lead singer. In 1973 the band began making limited pressings of their jam sessions, eventually releasing nine albums that were sold at the Source Restaurant for ten dollars each. The original recordings have become valuable to collectors of underground music. Celebrities such as Earth, Wind & Fire would buy Source records out of the back of the restaurant. Other family musicians formed various bands including "Spirit of 76", "Savage Sons of Yahowha" and "Breath". Death On December 26, 1974, the Source Family sold their restaurant and moved to Hawaii. On August 25, 1975, despite having no previous hang-gliding experience, YaHoWha used a hang glider to leap off a 1,300-foot (400 m) cliff on the eastern shore of Oahu. He crash-landed on the beach suffering no external injuries, but was unable to move and died nine hours later. After three days of vigil, YaHoWha was cremated and his ashes put to rest at Lanikai Beach in Hawaii. Legacy In 2006, two Source Family members, Isis Aquarian and Electricity Aquarian, wrote the history of the religious group. A revised version of the book entitled The Source: The Untold Story of Father Yod, Ya Ho Wa 13 and The Source Family was released in 2007 by Process Media , and included a CD with live Ya Ho Wa 13 performances, radio interviews, and Family recordings. The Source Foundation was set up at www.yahowha.org and released lost family music through Drag City Records, Fathers Morning Meditation Tapes through Global Recording Artist, a comic book, and The Source Family in 2012, co-directed by Jodi Wille and Maria Demopoulous. He introduced his version of Kundalini yoga to the United States. He was the spiritual director of the 3HO (Healthy, Happy, Holy Organization) foundation (and business ventures ), with over 300 centers in 35 countries. [ 3 ] He was accused of sexual abuse by several dozen of his female followers; an investigation called the Olive Branch Report found the allegations most likely true. [ 4 ] [ 5 ] Biography [ edit ] Early life [ edit ] Harbhajan Singh Khalsa was born on August 26, 1929, into a Sikh family in Kot Harkarn, Gujranwala district in the province of Punjab (now in Pakistan). His father, Dr. Kartar Singh Puri, served the British Raj as a medical doctor. His mother was named Harkrishan Kaur. His father was raised in the Sikh tradition and young Harbhajan was educated in a Catholic school run by nuns. Singh learned the fundamentals of Sikhism from his paternal grandfather, Sant Bhai Fateh Singh. Theirs was a well-to-do landlord family, owning most of their village in the foothills of the Himalayas . [ 6 ] Singh's schooling was interrupted in 1947 by the violent partition of India , when he and his family fled to New Delhi as refugees. There, Harbhajan Singh attended Camp College – a hastily put together arrangement for thousands of refugee students – and was an active member of the Sikh Students Federation in Delhi. [ 7 ] Four years later, he graduated with a master's degree in economics. [ 8 ] In 1953, Singh entered the service of the Government of India. He served in the Revenue Department, where his duties took him all over India. Eventually, Harbhajan Singh was promoted to a customs inspector at Delhi Airport . [ 9 ] In his final years in India, he also learned from Baba Virsa Singh at Gobind Sadan Institute. [ 10 ] In 1968, Singh emigrated to Toronto , Canada equipped with an endorsement from that country's High Commissioner to India, James George , who was also a student of his. [ 11 ] Harbhajan Singh made a considerable impact in the predominantly Anglo-Saxon metropolis. In three months, he established classes at several YMCAs , co-founded a yoga centre, was interviewed for national press and television, and helped set in motion the creation of eastern Canada's first Sikh temple in time for Guru Nanak 's five hundredth birthday the following year. [ 12 ] [ 13 ] Healthy, Happy, Holy Organization [ edit ] Main article: 3HO 1970 gathering at Santa Clara Canyon, New Mexico In 1969, Singh established the 3HO (Healthy, Happy, Holy Organization) Foundation in Los Angeles , California to further his missionary work. His brand of Sikhism appealed to the hippies who formed the bulk of his early converts. The Sikh practice of not cutting one's hair or beard was already accepted by the hippie culture. Singh encouraged vegetarianism even though Sikhs are traditionally meat eaters. Singh called the hippie youth 'searching souls' who wanted to experience elevated states of awareness and wanted to feel they were contributing to a world of peace and social justice. [ 14 ] He offered them all these things with vigorous yoga, an embracing holistic vision, and an optimistic spirit of sublime destiny. [ 15 ] Interest in yoga increased worldwide at this time. [ 16 ] To serve the changing times, Singh created the International Kundalini Yoga Teachers Association, dedicated to setting standards for teachers and the propagation of the teachings. [ 17 ] In 1994, the 3HO Foundation joined the United Nations as a non-governmental organization in consultative status with the Economic and Social Council, representing women's issues, promoting human rights, and providing education about alternative systems of medicine. [ 18 ] Other activities [ edit ] With Sant Fateh Singh 1971 Singh incorporated the storyline of the dawning new age into his teachings, a case of melding Western astrology with Sikh tradition. He proclaimed that " Guru Nanak was the Guru for the Aquarian Age ." It was, he declared, to be an age where people first experienced God, then believed, rather than the old way of believing and then being liberated by one's faith. [ 19 ] [ 20 ] With A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada and Sushil Kumar (Jain monk) , San Francisco 1975 Meeting Pope John Paul II at the Vatican, 1984 In the summer of 1970, Singh participated in an informal "Holy Man Jam" at the University of Colorado at Boulder with Swami Satchidananda (another Eastern yogi who has been accused of sexual abuse of his students), Stephen Gaskin of The Farm in Tennessee, Zen Buddhist Jakusho Kwong , and other local spiritual leaders. A few weeks later, he organized a gathering of spiritual teachers to engage and inspire the 200,000 attendees of the Atlanta International Pop Festival on the stage between the performances of the bands. [ 21 ] When U.S. President Nixon called drugs America's "Number one domestic problem", Singh launched a pilot program with two longtime heroin addicts in Washington, D.C., in 1972. The program attempted to treat heroin addiction through the practice of yoga and the consumption of garlic juice. [ 22 ] In 1984 he started the Yogi Tea brand. [ 23 ] Death [ edit ] Congressman Tom Udall with Harbhajan Singh Khalsa's widow, "Bibiji" Harbhajan Singh died of complications of heart failure at his home in Española , New Mexico , on October 6, 2004, aged 75. He was survived by his wife, sons, daughter and five grandchildren. [ 24 ] Obituaries appeared in The Los Angeles Times , [ 25 ] the Times of India , [ 26 ] The New York Times , [ 24 ] and Yoga Journal . [ 27 ] Khalsa's passing was noted by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee , which closed its offices to commemorate his death. [ 28 ] The State of New Mexico honoured him by renaming State Highway 106 as the Yogi Bhajan Memorial Highway. [ 29 ] The New Mexico Government flew its flags at half-mast for two days (Oct 7–8) in his honour after his death on Oct 6, and declared Oct 23 "Yogi Bhajan Memorial Day". [ 30 ] Allegations of sexual abuse [ edit ] See also: Sexual abuse by yoga gurus In 2019, Yogi Bhajan's former secretary Pamela Saharah Dyson published the book Premka: White Bird in a Golden Cage: My Life with Yogi Bhajan , reporting that she and other women had abusive [ 31 ] sexual relationships with Harbhajan Singh. [ 32 ] [ 31 ] In March 2020, the Siri Singh Sahib Corporation commissioned An Olive Branch (AOB) to look into allegations of sexual abuse and rape of female followers and assistants. The AOB report, published in August, found that it was "more likely than not" that Yogi Bhajan raped three women, injured eight women during sex, engaged in nonconsensual touching of nine people, showed pornography to minors, used sexually offensive language, directed women to shave their pubic hair, and directed women to have sex with other women, that his followers' claims that he was celibate were inaccurate, and that he "employed a variety of methods to control his students including compartmentalization, quid pro quo, promises, threats, slander, phone calls, guarding, and/or telling women they were his wife." [ 33 ] The report acknowledged "the convictions of Yogi Bhajan's Supporters as accurate representations of their beliefs" rather than deliberate falsehoods. [ 33 ] Soon after, other media published stories based on the report that considered the allegations to be true. [ 34 ] Reception [ edit ] Media coverage [ edit ] In 1977, Time published a critical article, titled "Yogi Bhajan's Synthetic Sikhism". [ 35 ] The article alleged that Gurucharan Singh Tohra, former President of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), had stated that Harbhajan Singh is not the leader of Sikhism in the Western World as he claimed, and that Tohra had denied the SGPC had ever given Singh the title of Siri Singh Sahib. [ 35 ] Harbhajan Singh is featured in books discussing the successes of Sikhs who migrated from India to the West, including Surjit Kaur's Among the Sikhs: Reaching for the Stars . [ 36 ] and Gurmukh Singh's The Global Indian: The Sikhs . [ 37 ] Scholars' views [ edit ] Scholars including Verne A. Dusenbery and Pashaura Singh have concurred that Harbhajan Singh's introduction of Sikh teachings into the West helped identify Sikhism as a world religion while at the same time creating a compelling counter-narrative to that which identified Sikhs solely as a race with a shared history in India. [ 38 ] [ 39 ] [ 40 ] Philip Deslippe, a historian of American religion, wrote a 2012 article "From Maharaj to Mahan Tantric: The Construction of Yogi Bhajan's Kundalini Yoga", using 3HO source archive material and news articles to reveal how Harbhajan Singh recreated his own story after his first trip back to India: [ 10 ] I set out to answer the question "where did Kundalini Yoga as taught by Yogi Bhajan (KYATBYB) come from?" and not much else. I tried to support my findings with as much evidence as possible, and for that evidence to be as clear, specific, verifiable, and close to the source, such as interviews with first hand witnesses (Pamela being one of them), quotes from Yogi Bhajan, contemporary newspaper accounts, and exercises taken from manuals. I concluded that in the early years of 3HO, Yogi Bhajan was using the physical yoga of Swami Dhirendra Brahmachari and the persona and mantra of Baba Virsa Singh, and that the figure of Sant Hazara Singh only became prominent after the first trip to India in 1970-1971 when Yogi Bhajan had a falling out with Virsa Singh. — Philip Deslippe [ 10 ] Television [ edit ] In 2024, HBO ran the series Breath of Fire , which explores Yogi Bhajan's mental and sexual abuse of his followers. raw_text: The Source Family Ara Eve Leo Sal 1x The Source Family was a short-lived spiritual commune in Los Angeles, active primarily from 1969 to 1975, founded by James Edward Baker (1922â1975), a former U.S. Marine and restaurateur who proclaimed himself Father Yod and later YaHoWha, attracting around 140 followers through a regimen of raw vegetarianism, Kundalini yoga, esoteric mysticism blending Kabbalah and Theosophy, communal living, and ritualistic practices including cannabis meditation and polyamorous relationships. [1] [2] [3] Baker, leveraging the success of his pioneering organic health food restaurant The Sourceâwhich generated up to $10,000 daily and drew celebrity patronsâexpanded the group into a self-sustaining community housed in a Hollywood Hills mansion, where members adhered to "spiritual law" over conventional norms, forgoing Western medicine and emphasizing purification through diet and discipline. [3] [1] The commune's musical output, recorded as the band Ya Ho Wa 13 with over a dozen psychedelic albums featuring improvisational rock and spiritual chants, represented a notable cultural artifact of the era, later reissued and influencing modern interest in countercultural esotericism. [2] [3] Controversies arose from Baker's authoritarian leadership, his harem of 14 wives, experimental sexual rites framed as sacred transformation, and incidents such as the hospitalization of a malnourished child due to dietary extremism, though the group avoided the violence associated with contemporaneous cults like the Manson Family. [2] [1] Following relocation to Hawaii in 1974, the commune dissolved after Baker's fatal hang-gliding accident on August 25, 1975, scattering members and leaving a legacy documented in member memoirs and a 2012 film, amid ongoing debates over whether it embodied utopian experimentation or coercive cult dynamics. [1] [3] Origins and Early History Founding of The Source Restaurant In 1969, Jim Baker, a former Marine, judo expert, and restaurateur, opened The Source Restaurant at 8301 Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles , transforming a former hamburger stand into a pioneering venue for organic vegetarian cuisine. [4] [5] The establishment launched on April 1, emphasizing raw, unprocessed foods inspired by ancient texts such as the Essene Gospel of Peace, which Baker interpreted as promoting health through plant-based diets excluding meat, dairy, and refined sugars. [6] [7] Baker's prior ventures, including the Aware Inn opened with his wife Elaine in 1957 , had introduced natural foods but lacked the explicit spiritual dimension that defined The Source. [8] Motivated by personal health advocacy and a shift toward esoteric teachings, he positioned the restaurant as a hub for holistic wellness, serving dishes like veggie burgers, nut milks, and sprouted grains to counterculture patrons including celebrities and hippies on the Sunset Strip . [7] [9] Staffed initially by young acolytes in white robes, the eatery quickly gained traction for its macrobiotic principles and ambiance blending Eastern mysticism with West Coast bohemianism , laying groundwork for Baker's emerging communal vision. [10] [1] The restaurant's success stemmed from its alignment with 1960s health trends, drawing crowds seeking alternatives to conventional diets amid rising interest in yoga , meditation , and organic living, though Baker's unorthodox promotionsâsuch as tying meals to spiritual enlightenmentâdistinguished it from secular health food outlets. [7] [11] By fostering a devoted following, The Source evolved from a commercial enterprise into the nucleus of what would become The Source Family, with profits funding communal activities and attracting members through shared meals and lectures. [10] [12] Jim Baker's Transformation into Father Yod James Edward Baker, born July 4, 1922, in Cincinnati , Ohio , and raised by his mother during the Great Depression , initially pursued physical and entrepreneurial paths after earning a Silver Star for valor in the U.S. Marines during the World War II Battle of Rennell Island . Postwar, he established a gym , relocated to Hollywood to operate a sandal shop, and founded multiple restaurants including the Aware Inn, Old World, and Discovery Inn, before launching The Sourceâa raw vegetarian venue on the Sunset Strip âon April 1, 1969. [13] Baker's exposure to health pioneers like Paul Bragg , the Nature Boys movement, Vedic texts, and occult scholar Manly P. Hall fostered early esoteric interests, but his profound spiritual shift occurred through Kundalini yoga under Yogi Bhajan , whom he met in May 1969 and regarded as his first true spiritual father. As Bhajan's disciple #1 in Southern California , Baker immersed himself in the yogi's neo-Sikh practices, experiencing an awakening that redirected his life from commercial success toward mystical authority, blending yogic energy work with Theosophical and Rosicrucian elements. [6] [13] [2] In March 1971, Baker consummated this evolution by adopting the name Father Yod (later Ya Ho Wha), growing long hair and a beard , donning white robes, and declaring himself a divine patriarch to an emerging commune of young followers attracted to The Source's countercultural vibe. This persona, which followers viewed as an enlightened guide capable of channeling cosmic forces, formalized his role as spiritual leader of what became the Source Family, with over 140 members living communally under his guidance by the mid-1970s. [13] [2] Leadership and Structure Biography of Father Yod (James Edward Baker) James Edward Baker was born on July 4, 1922, in Cincinnati , Ohio . [14] His early life included a reported abandonment by his father shortly after birth, though accounts vary on the circumstances of his father's death or departure. [15] During World War II , Baker served as a United States Marine Corps pilot, earning the Silver Star medal for gallantry in action, particularly at Guadalcanal , where he claimed to have shot down 13 Japanese aircraft. [16] [17] Postwar, he developed expertise in judo and jujitsu, competing successfully and having his hands legally registered as lethal weapons due to their proficiency in martial arts . [16] [17] In the late 1940s and 1950s, Baker pursued ambitions in Hollywood as a stuntman, auditioning unsuccessfully for the role of Tarzan in a film adaptation . [17] His pre-spiritual career involved documented criminal activity, including the 1955 killing of a man in a judo confrontation and a 1963 manslaughter conviction for another fatal altercation; he also admitted to robbing between two and eleven banks during this period. [17] By the 1960s, Baker shifted toward health and wellness, influenced by proto-hippie groups like the Nature Boys and practices such as yoga and raw vegetarianism . He opened two pioneering vegetarian restaurants on the Sunset Strip , including The Source in 1969, which gained popularity among celebrities such as John Lennon , Joni Mitchell , and Marlon Brando for its organic, macrobiotic fare. [17] [13] Baker's transformation into Father Yod occurred around 1971, following a profound spiritual awakening he described as enlightenment, leading him to renounce material wealth, grow a long beard, and adopt flowing robes. He founded the Source Family, a commune initially based in the Hollywood Hills that grew to over 140 members, emphasizing communal living, esoteric teachings blending Eastern mysticism, Kabbalah , and ancient astronaut theories, and tantric practices. Baker positioned himself as a patriarchal guru , engaging in polygamy with 14 wivesâprimarily young women from the groupâand fathering at least seven children, while enforcing strict hierarchies and rituals among followers who surrendered personal assets to the collective. [17] [18] On August 25, 1975, at age 53, Baker died in a hang gliding accident on Oahu, Hawaii , when his untested glider stalled after launching from a 400-meter cliff without prior training or lessons, despite warnings from experienced pilots; his body was cremated, with ashes scattered. [14] [17] The event occurred amid the Source Family's relocation to Hawaii , where financial strains and internal dissent had begun eroding the group's cohesion. [18] Internal Hierarchy and Membership The Source Family operated under a patriarchal hierarchy centered on James Edward Baker, known as Father Yod , who positioned himself as the absolute spiritual authority and "earthly spiritual father" to all members. [19] Obedience to Father Yod was codified in core rules that every member memorized, including prioritizing love and adherence to his teachings above all else, which reinforced his unchallenged leadership . [19] Beneath him, a council composed of his wivesâeventually numbering 14, such as Ahom (his first wife), Isis Aquarian, Prism, and Harvest âfunctioned as a matriarchal advisory body, influencing family decisions and serving as "mothers of the Family." [20] [21] These women, selected by Father Yod , held significant informal power in communal governance , though ultimate authority remained with him. [22] Membership peaked at around 140 individuals in the mid-1970s, primarily young adults drawn from the Los Angeles counterculture scene, including hippies and health-conscious seekers attracted initially through the Source Restaurant. [23] [24] Joining required full commitment, often involving liquidation of personal assets, adoption of new names ending in "Aquarian," and public vows of loyalty to Father Yod as spiritual father, which effectively severed prior ties and integrated recruits into the commune's collective living in Hollywood Hills mansions. [23] [1] Men and women adhered to gender-specific roles emphasizing complementary spiritual functions, with women often focused on nurturing and ritual support, while men handled physical labor and protection, though these were subordinated to the group's overarching devotion to Father Yod . [22] Retention relied on daily rituals and economic interdependence via the restaurant, but the structure's intensity led to high turnover, with some estimates suggesting numbers fluctuated into the low hundreds at times due to recruitment via celebrity patrons. [25] Beliefs and Practices Spiritual Teachings and Syncretism The spiritual teachings of the Source Family revolved around Father Yod's self-proclaimed role as the earthly manifestation of divine paternity, positioning him as the central authority for spiritual guidance and communal obedience. Members adhered to doctrines emphasizing unconditional love and submission to Yod, including commandments to obey his teachings, prioritize love for him over self-interest, and avoid harming fellow family members physically, emotionally, or spiritually. These principles framed Yod as a conduit to cosmic wisdom, with daily practices such as early-morning meditations, breathwork, and chanting "YaHoWah"âa variant of the Hebrew tetragrammaton for Godâaimed at awakening higher consciousness and interdimensional awareness. The group anticipated the Age of Aquarius as a transformative era, with Source Family children destined to lead humanity's spiritual evolution, reflecting Yod's vision of a utopian "tribe" fostering telepathy and collective enlightenment. [19] [1] Syncretism defined the Source Family's belief system, blending Eastern and Western esoteric traditions into a eclectic framework tailored to 1970s California counterculture . Core influences included Kundalini yoga practices derived from Yogi Bhajan , emphasizing energy activation through breath, posture, and ritual; Essene gospels for communal purity and natural living; Rosicrucian and Theosophical mysticism for occult knowledge; and astrological emphases on Aquarian renewal. Yod incorporated teachings from occultist Manly P. Hall and Freemasonic symbolism, alongside health-oriented inspirations from the Nature Boys movement, which promoted raw foods and vitality as paths to divinity. This fusion extended to neo-Tantric elements, such as "Dionysian" rituals involving sacred cannabis use and controlled sexual practices for kundalini elevation, often likened to seed retention techniques in historical groups like the Oneida Community . [2] [1] The syncretic approach lacked formal orthodoxy, prioritizing experiential "vibrations" over doctrinal rigidity, which allowed Yod to adapt elements like Atlantean lore and holistic death acceptanceâexemplified by the 3.5-day vigil over his body post-1975 hang-gliding death âas organic extensions of life's cycle. While insider accounts, such as those from chronicler Isis Aquarian, portray these teachings as profoundly liberating, external analyses highlight their opportunistic eclecticism, potentially exploiting members' search for meaning amid cultural upheaval. No peer-reviewed theological studies exist, but journalistic reconstructions from participant testimonies underscore the blend's role in sustaining the commune's eight-year span from 1969 to 1977. [2] [26] Daily Rituals and Lifestyle Members of The Source Family adhered to a highly structured daily routine centered on spiritual discipline and communal synchronization, beginning with awakenings before 3:30 AM to prepare for morning meditation s commencing at 4:00 AM in a dedicated meditation room. [27] These sessions, led by Father Yod , featured esoteric teachings, life lessons, melodic chants invoking the "ancient, sacred Name of God," and a single inhalation of the sacred herb âidentified as marijuanaâto align vibrations with universal life energy. [27] [19] The meditations, often recorded by Isis Aquarian as the group's archivist, emphasized obedience to Father Yod 's guidance, with rules mandating love for the leader above self, non-harm to the body, and daily attunement to ascending cosmic currents through prescribed methods. [27] [19] Throughout the day, practices extended to physical and hygienic rituals, including ritual dips in the mansion's Olympic-sized outdoor swimming pool as part of a beauty regime, and water aerobics classes instructed by Father Yod to foster bodily purity and energy flow. [28] [1] The overall regimen resembled a spiritual boot camp, integrating tantric sexual practices viewed as sacred with disciplined labor, such as shifts at The Source Restaurant, to maintain self-sufficiency and group harmony. [29] [30] Dietary habits reflected a commitment to raw, vegetarian nutrition derived from the restaurant's health food ethos, avoiding cooked foods and emphasizing uncooked fruits, vegetables, nuts, and sprouted grains to preserve vital energies; Father Yod personally advocated recipes like raw cheesecakes. [4] Communal living enforced synchronized schedules to align members' energies, prohibiting individual deviations and requiring attendance at meditations alongside work duties, though the structure allowed for ecstatic musical sessions by Ya Ho Wa 13 to elevate group vibrations. [31] [31] This lifestyle, sustained from the late 1960s through the mid-1970s in Hollywood Hills mansions before relocation to Hawaii , prioritized collective spiritual evolution over personal autonomy. [1] Communal Operations Living Arrangements and Relocations The Source Family initially established communal living quarters in Los Angeles , beginning with a Georgian-style mansion in the Los Feliz neighborhood, constructed in 1914, which accommodated approximately 100 members for meditation, music sessions, and shared activities from 1972 to March 1973. [32] Members lived, worked, and slept communally in this three-story structure equipped with a swimming pool , reflecting the group's emphasis on collective spiritual and daily practices. [3] By March 1973, the group relocated within Los Angeles to a three-bedroom house in Nichols Canyon, near the Sunset Strip , expanding capacity to around 140 members through modifications such as outdoor sleeping platforms, attic conversions, and "cubbyholes"âwooden bunk structures installed in rooms and hallways. [32] This rented property, at $1,000 per month, included a pool, a dedicated band room, and a garage converted into a recording studio ; it served as the primary residence until circa 1974, during which 51 children were born to family members. [32] On December 26, 1974, following the sale of their Source Restaurant, the entire group of approximately 150 members relocated en masse from Los Angeles to Hawaii , seeking a tropical environment aligned with Father Yod's preferences. [3] They first settled on Kauai by January 15, 1975, occupying acreage centered around a main house for communal living, though a small contingent remained briefly in Los Angeles to finalize the restaurant transition. [20] Local reception on Kauai proved hostile, amid broader resident fatigue with communal groups like the nearby Taylor Camp . [33] Subsequently, the family shifted to Lanikai on Oahu, where they maintained communal arrangements until Father Yod's death on August 25, 1975; his ashes were interred at Lanikai Beach following a three-day vigil. [34] Financial difficulties and ongoing local antagonism exacerbated challenges in Hawaii, contributing to the group's fragmentation after the leader's passing. [35] Economic Model and Self-Sufficiency The Source Family's economic foundation relied heavily on The Source restaurant, established by Jim Baker on April 1 , 1969 , in Hollywood, California , which specialized in organic vegetarian cuisine and attracted countercultural clientele including celebrities. By 1974, the restaurant generated approximately $500,000 in annual revenueâequivalent to over $3 million in contemporary termsâproviding the primary income stream for the commune's operations and enabling support for more than 140 members. Profits were pooled collectively, with Baker redirecting earnings from the business he owned back into communal needs such as housing, food, and transportation, including luxury items like a white Rolls-Royce, which distinguished the group from more austere communes of the era. Communal labor underpinned the model, as members performed roles in restaurant service, kitchen work, and maintenance, fostering a structure where personal finances were surrendered to the collective under the organization's non-profit religious status. This arrangement sustained daily operations in Los Angeles, including residence in a rented Los Feliz mansion housing over 100 individuals, without dependence on government assistance or external philanthropy , though the influx of restaurant patrons also served as a recruitment mechanism for expanding membership. In September 1973, Baker proposed selling The Source to relocate the group to Hawaii for enhanced self-sufficiency through agrarian living, culminating in the restaurant's sale on December 26, 1974, and phased moves beginning that month to islands including Molokai, Kauai, and the Big Island. Initial outposts like Source Paia on Maui in summer 1973 aimed at local food production and commerce, but post-relocation effortsâsuch as the June 1975 establishment of Goodies Bakery and the "Father and Sons United Labor Force" for income generationâencountered resource shortages and failed to achieve independence, exacerbating financial strains amid legal issues from California and leading to the commune's dispersal by 1977. Cultural and Artistic Output Ya Ho Wa 13 Music and Recordings Ya Ho Wa 13, the musical ensemble of The Source Family, formed in the early 1970s as a vehicle for channeling spiritual vibrations through sound, with Father Yod (James Edward Baker) frequently contributing vocals, chants, or guidance during sessions. [36] The band consisted of commune members, described as "Hollywood misfits," who improvised psychedelic rock infused with tribal percussion, distorted guitars, and extended jams, often without prior rehearsal. [37] Recordings occurred in a soundproofed garage studio after 3:00 to 6:00 a.m. meditation sessions, reflecting the group's emphasis on ecstatic, trance-like expression over conventional composition. [38] Between 1973 and 1974, the group produced over 60 full-length albums during an 11-month period of intense activity, though masters for many were lost, limiting initial distribution. [39] Nine vinyl LPs were pressed on the commune's Higher Key Records label and sold exclusively through The Source restaurant in Los Angeles , featuring raw, experimental tracks that blended acid rock with spiritual incantations. [39] Notable releases included Penetration: An Aquarian Symphony (1974), characterized by its lengthy, elemental-themed improvisations such as "Yod He Vau He" (11:25) and "Ya Ho Wha" (13:24), and Ya Ho Wha (1974), emphasizing unrehearsed psychedelic explorations. [40] Sky Saxon of The Seeds , who joined the Family in 1973, contributed to select recordings, adding garage rock elements. [38] Following Father Yod's death in 1975, surviving members continued under the Ya Ho Wa 13 name, releasing Golden Sunrise (1977) on Fire Water Air Recordsâmarking the debut of post-Yod material with Saxon's prominent vocalsâand Yodship (1977), which honored the leader's legacy through reflective jams. [36] These efforts totaled around 14 known LPs from the era, preserved in limited runs. [41] In the 2000s , archival reissues by labels like Swordfish and Prophase revived interest among psychedelic enthusiasts, compiling unreleased tapes into sets such as the 13-CD box of complete available '70s recordings, highlighting the music's raw, unpolished intensity. [41] Sacred Bones Records later curated selections, including a 2020s LP of original tracks tied to Family scrapbooks, underscoring the recordings' niche appeal in underground psych and experimental scenes rather than mainstream success. [42] The output's improvisational nature, rooted in communal rituals, prioritized vibrational transmission over commercial viability, with empirical listenership confined to cult followers and later collectors. [36] Influence on Counterculture and Health Food Trends The Source Restaurant, established by James Edward Baker (Father Yod) in 1969 at 8301 Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles , served as a pioneering venue for organic vegetarian cuisine, attracting celebrities and countercultural figures with its raw, plant-based offerings prepared by robed commune members. [1] [7] This establishment popularized health-focused eating in Southern California during the late 1960s and early 1970s, predating widespread mainstream adoption of vegan and raw food diets by emphasizing unprocessed, natural ingredients as integral to spiritual purity and physical vitality. [4] [10] The restaurant's success, generating revenue to sustain the commune, helped normalize vegetarianism among urban elites and hippies, contributing to the shift from meat-centric American diets toward plant-based alternatives that later influenced broader wellness trends. [24] [43] Beyond nutrition, the Source Family embodied countercultural experimentation through communal living, esoteric syncretism , and artistic output, including the psychedelic rock collective Ya Ho Wa 13, which recorded nine albums between 1973 and 1975 featuring improvisational, ritualistic soundscapes sold directly at the restaurant . [19] [44] These recordings, blending Eastern mysticism with Western rock influences, reflected and amplified the era's rejection of materialism in favor of ecstatic, guru-led spirituality , resonating with the broader hippie movement's embrace of yoga , free love , and alternative fashion. [1] [45] The group's promotion of these elements via the restaurant and music helped seed enduring California lifestyle staples, though their insular, hierarchical structure limited direct emulation compared to more decentralized countercultural streams. [46] [47] Controversies and Criticisms Allegations of Exploitation and Abuse Critics and select former members have accused Jim Baker, known as Father Yod , of financial exploitation within The Source Family, claiming he required members to donate all personal assets upon joining and to provide unpaid labor at the communal restaurant, The Source, which generated revenue primarily benefiting the group's hierarchy and Baker's personal indulgences, including a harem of wives and access to private aircraft. [48] [49] These practices, according to detractors, created a system of economic dependency, where members' contributions funded the commune's operations and Baker's lifestyle without equitable return or exit options for accumulated wealth. [48] Allegations of psychological and sexual abuse center on Baker's authoritarian control over members' personal lives, particularly women, whom he reportedly directed in their "utilization" for service to men, expecting unquestioning obedience and framing dissent as spiritual failure. [48] Former participants have described imposed sexual rituals as forms of physical and psychological power abuse, with Baker objectifying women by referring to some as his "milk cows" and assigning roles that prioritized male leaders' needs over individual autonomy. [48] One ex-member recounted being expelled from the group in 1972 following a minor disagreement with Baker, characterizing the incident as emblematic of his abusive temperament and intolerance for challenge. [50] Concerns regarding child welfare include claims of neglect, such as withholding conventional medical treatment in favor of spiritual remedies and inadequate care for dependents, which some attribute to the commune's insular ideology prioritizing obedience to Baker over external standards of health and safety. [48] A reported case involved a mentally ill bookkeeper being abandoned in a Hawaii hotel during the group's relocation in the mid-1970s, highlighting alleged disregard for vulnerable members' needs amid logistical shifts. [48] These accusations contrast with accounts from many long-term ex-members who, in the 2012 documentary The Source Family , emphasize voluntary participation and personal growth, suggesting a divide in retrospective evaluations influenced by post-exit deprogramming or lingering loyalty. [48] Polygamy, Free Love, and Power Dynamics Father Yod , the charismatic leader of the Source Family commune established in Los Angeles in 1969 , practiced polygamy by taking 13 to 14 "spiritual wives," many of whom were young women in their late teens or early twenties while he was in his fifties. [51] [21] These unions were framed as part of a spiritual path emphasizing tantric energy and communal harmony, with Yod selecting wives such as Isis Aquarian and Venus Aquarian to form an inner circle . [4] Early in the commune's history, the group espoused free love influenced by 1960s counterculture , allowing members multiple partners as a means of transcending ego and fostering group unity, though Yod later adjusted rules to centralize sexual access around himself, creating a de facto harem structure. [21] Power dynamics within the Source Family revolved around Yod's absolute authority, often described by former members and documentarians as a "benevolent dictatorship," where he dictated relocations, renamed individuals (e.g., followers as Isis or Electricity), and enforced communal norms like vegetarianism and raw food diets. [21] [52] To delegate operations as the group grew to over 140 members by the early 1970s, Yod established a council of his 13 wives in the "Father House" phase, ostensibly shifting toward matriarchal governance for daily decisions while retaining veto power and spiritual oversight. [21] This structure masked underlying imbalances, as Yod's charisma and claims of divine incarnation compelled obedience, with dissenters facing expulsion; for instance, his legal wife Robin Popper (renamed Ahom) publicly rejected the polygamy as a "lust trip" by a "dirty old man," leading to her departure. [4] The interplay of polygamy and free love amplified hierarchical tensions, as Yod's exclusive access to multiple partners contrasted with restrictions on other men, who were sometimes paired with older or less desirable women under communal matching, fostering resentment among some male members. [19] Empirical accounts from survivors highlight causal links between these dynamics and exploitation risks: Yod's encouragement of "mystical sex" for spiritual elevation prioritized his vision over individual consent , with underage female recruits occasionally married to older men per his guidance, though no widespread legal prosecutions ensued due to the era's lax oversight of consensual adult communes. [53] While proponents like Isis Aquarian viewed the arrangements as liberating from monogamous norms, critics within and outside the group, including in post-dissolution reflections, attribute the commune's internal fractures to unchecked leader privilege, evidenced by departures like Zarathustra's refusal to relocate to Hawaii in 1974. [4] [54] Comparisons to Other Cults and Empirical Assessments The Source Family exhibited hallmarks of charismatic new religious movements prevalent in the 1970s counterculture , including devotion to a self-proclaimed enlightened leader, communal resource sharing, and syncretic spiritual practices blending Eastern mysticism with Western esotericism . However, it differed markedly from destructive cults like the Manson Family , which, under Charles Manson's influence, orchestrated the Tate-LaBianca murders on August 8-10, 1969, resulting in nine deaths; contemporaries occasionally conflated the two due to their Los Angeles bases and unconventional lifestyles, but the Source emphasized pacifism , health food enterprises, and artistic output without recorded violence. [24] [55] In contrast to the Rajneeshpuram commune led by Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, which grew to over 7,000 residents by 1985 and involved documented criminality such as the 1984 bioterrorism incident using salmonella to influence electionsâaffecting 751 peopleâthe Source Family, peaking at around 140 members between 1971 and 1975, prioritized self-sufficiency through raw food restaurants like The Source on Sunset Strip, which attracted celebrities without resorting to fraud or attacks. Both groups practiced polygamy and "free love" under the guru's authority, yet the Source's model dissolved non-violently after leader Jim Baker's (Father Yod) death on August 25, 1975, in a hang-gliding crash, avoiding the Rajneesh movement's federal indictments and deportation of its leader in 1985. [56] Empirical evaluations, primarily from former member testimonies in documentaries and interviews rather than large-scale studies, reveal mixed long-term impacts: approximately 100-140 participants experienced hierarchical devotion that some credited for fostering discipline and creativity, leading to post-dissolution pursuits in music, health advocacy, and entrepreneurship , with no mass casualties or suicides akin to Jonestown's 918 deaths in 1978. Critics, including ex-members, highlight psychological dependencies and unequal power dynamics, though outcomes showed resilience, as many reintegrated into society by the late 1970s , with diverse trajectories from alternative spirituality to conventional lives, contrasting the alienation in groups like Heaven's Gate , which culminated in 39 suicides in 1997. The absence of felony convictions or victim litigation post-1975 underscores a lower destructiveness threshold compared to peers, though archival self-reports from adherents like archivist Isis Aquarian may overstate positives due to insider perspectives. [35] [44] [25] Decline and Aftermath The Hang-Gliding Incident and Death of Father Yod On August 25, 1975, James Edward Baker , known as Father Yod or Ya Ho Wha, attempted a hang-gliding flight from a 1,300-foot cliff on Oahu, Hawaii , despite having no prior experience with the activity. [17] [24] The maneuver was undertaken shortly after the Source Family's relocation to Hawaii , amid reports that Baker had been discussing his physical departure from the group in the preceding days while gathered with his wives at a house in Lanikai. [33] During the flight, the glider stalled, causing Baker to crash into the Pacific Ocean below. [17] [24] Baker sustained severe injuries in the impact and was rescued from the water, but he succumbed nine hours later at approximately 5:15 p.m. local time. [6] [18] Members of the Source Family interpreted the event through a spiritual lens, with some accounts from participants claiming Baker "left his earthly body at will," framing the accident as a deliberate ascension rather than a miscalculation of risk . [6] [57] Independent reporting, however, attributes the death to the inherent dangers of unauthorized hang-gliding, noting Baker's lack of training and the sport's history of fatalities in Hawaii during that era, including other incidents linked to fringe groups experimenting with aerial feats. [58] [17] The incident marked a pivotal rupture for the Source Family, as Baker's death at age 53 removed the central charismatic authority , accelerating the commune's fragmentation despite prior preparations for his absence. [59] [35] His remains were cremated, with ashes scattered at Lanikai Beach on Oahu. [18] [14] Dissolution of the Commune Following the death of Father Yod on August 25, 1975, in a hang-gliding accident off a cliff in Oahu, Hawaii , the Source Family experienced a leadership vacuum that eroded its communal cohesion. [60] [24] The group, which had relocated en masse to Hawaii from Los Angeles shortly after Christmas 1974, attempted to sustain operations without its charismatic founder, but internal fractures emerged rapidly due to the absence of centralized authority. [3] [13] Financial strains exacerbated the instability, as the sale of the Source Restaurant in Los Angeles had funded ill-advised purchases including a fishing boat and an airplane intended for spotting fish stocks, leaving the commune with depleted resources and mounting stress among members. [13] Without Yod's directive influence, disputes over succession and daily governance intensified, leading to a gradual splintering where members began dispersing to pursue individual lives rather than adhering to collective rituals and self-sufficiency. [44] By 1978, the commune had fully disbanded, with former adherents reintegrating into mainstream society, though some retained personal spiritual practices derived from the group's teachings. [1] [60] The dissolution marked the end of the Source Family's structured existence after approximately eight years, reflecting the challenges of maintaining utopian communes dependent on a single leader's vision. [1] Legacy and Modern Perspectives Archival Preservation and Revivals Isis Aquarian, a former member and one of Father Yod's wives, has acted as the principal archivist for The Source Family , compiling and preserving collections of photographs, films, audio recordings, and scrapbooks documenting the commune's daily life and rituals from 1972 to 1977. [61] These materials, originally maintained on cassettes and other analog formats, form the core of the group's historical record. [62] The Source Foundation, co-founded by Aquarian and Electricity Aquarian on February 20, 2002, has coordinated preservation initiatives, including the reissuance of key texts such as "The Source: The Untold Story of Father Yod, Ya Ho Wa 13 and The Source Family" in August 2007 and "The Legend of Father and The Source Family" in September 2006. [62] In 2011, the foundation launched an online library featuring morning meditation tapes recorded during the commune's era. [62] Archival holdings were further secured by transferring approximately 50 boxes of materials to the University of California , Santa Barbara's Hamilton Library American Religions Collection around 2013. [1] Music from Ya Ho Wha 13 has undergone re-mastering from original tapes preserved in Aquarian's archives, with reissues including "The Lovers and the Chariot" in November 2003 and "The Operetta" in October 2004 via the Source Foundation, alongside later efforts supervised by Aquarian for Drag City Records. [62] [61] Surviving band members performed live in November 2007 and March 2008, reviving the group's psychedelic sound. [62] Revival efforts encompass media productions drawing on these archives, notably the documentary "The Source Family," directed by Jodi Wille and Maria Demopoulos, which premiered at SXSW on March 11, 2012, and received a theatrical release in May 2013, with Aquarian serving as associate producer.
