Â© 2022 Born James Edward Baker, but in his full charismatic bloom, Father Yod, and, before his untimely death, YaHoWha, he led the counterculture commune, the Source Family, in Los Angeles in the late 1960s and early 70s that for a time owned a wildly successful health food restaurant on Sunset Boulevard. His tight-knit clan thrived in the cultural permissiveness of Southern California, which gave cover to a hedonistic, patriarchal lifestyle that cemented his fame and notoriety. His checkered past and tendentious emphasis on sexual relations (âballingâ) as the very core to human life, including between adults and minors, brought unwanted publicity and public scorn. He remains a figure of mystery and great controversy, despite, as social historian Erik Davis suggests, his transforming âsex, drugs and rock ân roll into a genuine religion.â [1] Â His social ethos places him in a long line of American spirito-cultural entrepreneurs that test the outer limits of religious faith and interrogate the foundational tenets of a repressive, conformist utilitarian society. Â§ Â§ Â§ M any fringe religious figures fill American history, but few quite like James Baker/Father Yod/YaHoWha as he came to be known. Baker is one of those unfathomable, charismatic figures who both represent an era but also help define it, but whose hold over less critical and counterculture-focused minds in the late 1960s and early 1970s in Los Angeles cannot and should not be exaggerated. Like a Federico Fellini film character, he dashes in and out of moral sanity, one moment a pathetic imitation of a wise, penitent guru, the other a rather crude and lustful middle-aged man screwing teenagers. Itâs hard to tell the difference between the two selves, so full of contradiction and venality gather into one being, yet also a figure who shrewdly knew the basest, darkest corners of human reality and the strange power he acquired from this knowledge. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â He was a womanizer who craved sex. It got him into scrapes, in one case, leading to the death of a jealous husband. Then he discovered that he could become a guru figure with all the sex he wanted, and then some, with young, nubile women. The Source Family was born from âa deeply devoted group of young people, living communally, whose eccentric sexual, spiritual and financial relationships were commanded by an enormously charismatic patriarchal figure who presented himself to his flock as Father and God.â [2] Â Genius? Rogue? Scam artist? The elephant has many parts, but which one represents it best? Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â As a charismatic personality, Baker follows the classic pattern of a troubled upbringing that metamorphosed Â into a controversial yet well-publicized career. Thatâs the banner hanging on the shop window; go farther into the store and the realization emerges that he may have set a trap for anyone trying to analyze him, that it was not just charisma at work but the whole Baker/Yod/YaHoWha guru act a supreme joke played upon anyone who tries to dissect his curious life and whatever meaning can be squeezed out of it. Perhaps, at the end of a wild and dangerous hang-gliding ride that resulted in his untimely death, Baker discovered there was no meaning at all. If true, then he probably had the last laugh before tuning out the world for the final time. Â§ Â§ Â§ I s America uniquely placed to produce charismatic figures? Â Does its social permissiveness allow such personalities to find favor and fame in the racially divisive, culturally diverse, and morally unsettled reality that constitutes the United States since its birth? Perhaps it says something about the nationâs psycho-social vitality that figures of some disrepute can climb the slippery slopes of regenerative success and notoriety to achieve historical status (at least, briefly). This is certainly the case with James Edward Baker and his transformation into a spiritual guru of renown and controversy in the boiling cultural landscape that was Southern California in the 1960s and 70s merits examination. If there is a spigot of charisma, it can be easily found within Â the escapist and inchoate romp that was the Sixtiesâ counterculture movement. Baker was one of its most glaring examples. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Steve Allenâs Beloved Son: Â A Story of the Jesus Cults Â and Isis Aquarianâs Â (with Electricity Aquarian) The Source: Â The Untold Story of Father Yod, Ya Ho Wa 13 and the Source Family Â provide clear evidence of the difficult upbringing and its resultant charismatic trail that constitutes Bakerâs life. Like other charismatics, his introduction to harsh reality came at a young age, in Bakerâs case, as a baby. Â He was born, according to Aquarian, âat midnight on the fourth of July, in Cincinnati [Ohio] in 1922.â [3] Â His father was a firefighter who, shortly after Jim was born, walked out on the family, leaving his wife, Cora, to tend to a girl and the toddler by herself. The divorce deeply impacted his life, sending him on a lifelong quest, âfirst for his flesh father, and then later, as he matured, for his âSpiritual Father.ââ [4] Â Cora fed the family as a âhousekeeper and chefâ in both in private homes and institutions (the latter âtalent,â Allen claims, âthat was in time passed along to her sonâ [5] ). [6] Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â By the time Baker reached 10, the country had fallen into grim economic times. The Great Depression. Forced to work in odd jobs, âmostly hard labor,â he developed an âimpressive physique,â later pay romantic dividends. [7] Â Tall and attractive, he never shied away from difficult tasks. [8] Â The wheels of his personal history quickened with each passing year: as a teenager, employed by the Roosevelt Administrationâs Civilian Conservation Corps as a road and dam builder, among other jobs; at 16 winner of the Ohio State Archery Competition; married at 19 with a daughter to follow; off to World War II to become a decorated Marine, expert at hand-to-hand combat; Marine Corps judo champion; teacher in Idaho to Marine judo instructors and for a brief time owned a gym (âBaker Studio of Body Cultureâ [9] ). An eclectic career, no doubt, yet one that placed him in the very frontlines of masculine life. The remaining parts of the Baker body of work, as revealed below, became legends. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â While pained by the exodus of his father, Baker could turn to one family ancestor in the 19th century for inspiration: his great-grandfather, also Â named Jim Baker. This ancestor, his biographer claims, âfor sixty years of the Westâs most turbulent history was a prominent figure.â [10] Â Like his descendent decades later, Baker straddled two worlds â the pioneering one and the Native American Â one he came to love and adopt (which he claimed as the happiest of his life [11] ). Miracle cures and medicinal charms held sway for him, as it did for his namesake who practiced them under the guise of New Age spirituality. Prodigiously tall, the womanizing âMountain Manâ Baker roamed the wilderness in various guises â from trapper to guide and everything in between â fathering 14 children with Native American wives and 13 more with pioneering ones, like his restless descendant, leaving his mark in several places. While the biography chronicles his exploits, little is known about the fates and thoughts of the many wives and 27 children he left behind of the peripatetic biological husband/father. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â A moment in this peripatetic lifestyle stands out above the rest if only because it presaged much of his later destiny. Â He was 14 when he fell ill to hemorrhoids, necessitating an operation. Coincidentally, Paul Bragg (ânutritionist and health food pioneerâ [12] ) was traveling Â through Cincinnati on a Health Crusade at that exact moment. Bragg more than simply opened a new world for the young Baker; for a time, he even served as a substitute father, always part of the playbook of the rising charismatic. Jim invited Bragg to his house, the older man cooking a meal for him and his mother. The friendship extended for several years, as did Bakerâs growing belief in the power and impact of healthy, nutritional food on the human body. Since the hemorrhoids are not mentioned again, presumably he was cured of the affliction. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â The siren call of Hollywood beckoned. He sought the role of Tarzan, and not getting the part, married a second time (to a design artist named Elaine) and dabbled in the occult, astrology, and mysticism with his wife under the sway of Manly P. Hall, author of The Secret Teachings of All Ages . Hall, the product of an estranged relationship with his father who grew into a powerful charismatic in his own right, is the type of eccentric personality well represented in the annals of Americaâs alternative religio-spiritual movements. [13] Â His dramatic, biblical prophet-like headshots were designed to impress, or awe his audiences, even as they endowed him with the look of a deranged scientist. He charmed many with his earnestness and utter confidence in his beliefs, and influenced many others, including President Ronald Reagan. [14] Â The strength and power of Hallâs ideas should not be underestimated; they echo in major threads of our own culture today. Donald Trump was another believer and beneficiary of Hallâs ideas. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Hall was an entry point for the Bakers into the bohemian counterculture and its divergent beliefs. His fellow travelers included fitness guru Jack LaLanne and a group that came to be known as âNature Boys.â [15] Â According to Aquarian, these âNature Boys,â along with the east coast Beatniks, paved the way for the hippie movement. [16] Â To earn money, he created a business for the manufacture of leather belts and custom-made sandals. Beneath Bakerâs entrepreneurial faÃ§ade bubbled the desire to escape the Maya, or the quotidian daily reality, or the ârat raceâ for the rest of us. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Charismatic personalities seek the limelight and Los Angeles, like it has for so many others, provided the vehicle for the publicity he craved. Fame for Baker came in an unexpected way. The Bakers cared for a neighborâs dog in Topanga Canyon when its owner served three weeks of jail time in prison for âtraffic charges.â [17] Â The altercation started when the neighbor came to the Bakersâ home demanding Bakerâs help in moving his car. He also berated Baker for âallegedly mistreating his dog.â [18] Â Events suggest, at least, according to the Los Angeles Times , that the pitched argument intensified and by the time they reached the neighborâs car, the other man drew a hunting knife and pressed it against Bakerâs stomach. Whereupon the judo expert immediately grabbed the manâs wrist (his expertise prepared for such moments) and threw him over his shoulder, both landing in a gully. Baker judo-chopped the manâs neck until he saw the man was dead. Why Baker continued to hack the neighbor until he died (he could have stopped after one chop) was a question never answered. Elaine Baker and neighbors corroborated Jimâs side of the story, with a jury ruling in his favor (self-defense). Â A picture in the Times Â shows Elaine happily embracing the freed Baker. Life could return to normal, at least, Elaine hoped. Baker was back in normal society, and no longer just another anonymous, fame-hungry acolyte in Los Angeles. Â The publicity bug penetrated his skin, and he remained in its claws for the rest of his life. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â An issue that separates mystics from ordinary yokels is their adamant belief that western doctors cause more harm than good. This belief brought conflict between Elaine and Jim. When she got pregnant, he insisted on a natural birth at home while she preferred a hospital. She won the debate but got measles in the waiting room before delivering a deaf baby. Aquarian claims that Baker did his level best to heal the babyâs deafness by natural means (even getting a goat to provide more nutritional milk than Â what cows produce), but with apparently no improvement to the babyâs hearing. It didnât stop them from having two more children, and even opening a âgourmet health food restaurant,â apparently the first of its kind in the United States. [19] Â In 1958, the Aware Inn appeared at the perfect time to capture the growing interest in nutritional food but with the added twist of being served in a stylish upscale setting. Â§ Â§ Â§ I t was not simply that the Aware Inn was a trendy operation, jumping on the backs of a rising health food movement (or in Steve Allenâs words, âthe health food, natural-ingredients fadâ [20] ), but it was also located in the middle of Sunset Boulevard that caught the attention of passing movie stars as they drove by, including Steve McQueen, Paul Newman, Marlon Brando, and aging Greta Garbo (Baker claimed he had an affair with her [21] ). âJim prepare[d] the food during the day,â Aquarian claims, âand in the evenings, Elaine would co-host and Jim would drink half a bottle of vodka, cook for a while, and then go out and work the room.â How his proclivity for alcohol squared with his obsession with pure foods is never mentioned. A second Aware Inn was opened in San Fernando Valley, and later, the Old World on the Strip, all successful. With a flourishing chain of restaurants as his calling card, like all good charismatic personalities, Baker was absorbing the mores of his Hollywood surroundings, soon to excel in them. Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Â Paradise is never paradisiacal , at least, not for long. An inner restlessness, an inner hunger, a deep-seated angst that success is never enough, there cannot be enough fame â all these pervade the charismatic life . And so it was with Jim. He didnât care if he hurt othersâ feelings, in many respects the â otherâdidnât Â exist (a characteristic often associated with malignant narcissists, with whom many charismatics share traits). Â The charismatic also tests fate, and in coming out ahead, proclaims themselves invisible. As a local celebrity, Bakerâs roving bedroom eye found many willing participants; how this wounded his marriage and family he had little concern. Â The roulette ball stopped on âa blonde dancer turned television actress,â Jean Ingram, â31, gorgeous, and recently separated from her wealthy hotelier husband.â [22] Â Baker knew the Ingrams for two years as customers of his and Elaineâs restaurant. No wealth-as-of-date property is recorded, since neither the article nor its secondary quotation names a specific year for the peak within the restaurant's roughly five year operating span. 3 Origins Origin Period Well-attested to 1975 1 Origin Period Well-attested 1970s 2 Place of Origin Well-attested Los Angeles, United States 2 Founder Well-attested Jim Baker (Father Yod) 2 Status Status Today Well-attested Historical; not practised continuously 2 Disbanded by 1978 after Father Yod's death in 1975 Learn More A Los Angeles Commune Around a Health-Food Restaurant The Source Family was a communal spiritual group in Los Angeles in the early 1970s centered on Jim Baker , known to followers as Father Yod and later YaHoWha, a former restaurateur and martial artist. Unusually, the community supported itself through a genuinely successful and influential business: The Source , a popular health-food restaurant on the Sunset Strip that was among the pioneers of natural-foods dining in America and drew a celebrity clientele. The group blended an eclectic mix of Eastern mysticism, esoteric and Western spiritual currents, meditation and breathing practices, and communal living, and it produced a body of privately released psychedelic-rock recordings that later gained a cult following among collectors. Father Yod took the role of spiritual father to the community and, in a practice that drew criticism, had multiple "spiritual wives." The community was relatively short-lived: after relocating to Hawaii , it dispersed following Baker's death in 1975 from injuries sustained in a hang-gliding accident. The Source Family is remembered as a distinctive artifact of the Southern California counterculture, documented in a later book and film drawing on former members' accounts, and is generally discussed as a communal experiment of its era rather than as a group associated with the kinds of criminal harm found in some others. Father Yod's Death and the Family's Afterlife The Source Family left Los Angeles at its peak. Pressured by publicity, school authorities and neighbours, Jim Baker, by then called Father Yod and married within the group to thirteen spiritual wives, sold the Source restaurant's goodwill and moved his white robed household to Hawaii in 1974. The islands were unwelcoming, money ran short, and on 25 August 1975 Baker launched himself from a cliff over Waimanalo Bay on a hang glider he had never flown, landed hard on the beach, refused hospital treatment in accordance with his teachings, and died nine hours later. The Family, deprived of the man its whole cosmology orbited, dissolved within a few years. Its afterlife has been remarkable. The group's house band, Ya Ho Wha 13, had pressed small runs of improvised psychedelic records in the early 1970s, and those albums became prized by collectors, leading to reissues and even reunion performances decades later. Former members Isis Aquarian , the group's self appointed archivist, and Electricity Aquarian assembled the photographs, tapes and family chronicles into a 2007 book, The Source, and their archive underpinned the 2012 documentary The Source Family, which brought the commune a sympathetic second hearing. Scholars and journalists now treat the Family as a defining specimen of the Aquarian age commune, remembered by many alumni with affection and by others as a warning about surrendering judgment, whose restaurant, incidentally, helped invent health food dining in America. He founded a spiritual commune in the Hollywood Hills known as the Source Family. He was also lead singer of the commune's experimental psychedelic rock band, Ya Ho Wha 13 . Contents 1 Early life 2 Source Family 3 Music 4 Death 5 Legacy 6 References 7 Further reading 8 External links Early life [ ] James Edward Baker was born on July 4, 1922, in Cincinnati, Ohio. Baker earned the Silver Star as a United States Marine in World War II and became expert in Jujutsu . He moved to California to become a Hollywood stuntman and was influenced by the Nature Boys, a Los Angeles-based group of beats who lived a natural lifestyle, maintained vegetarian diets, and lived "according to Nature's Laws". [ 1 ] Baker also studied philosophy, religion and esoteric spiritual teachings, even becoming a Vedantic monk for a time. He later became a follower of Yogi Bhajan , a Sikh spiritual leader and teacher of Kundalini Yoga . In 1963, Baker was convicted of murdering the husband of actress Jean Ingram, with whom he was having an affair. [ 2 ] In 1969, Baker founded the Source Restaurant on Los Angeles's Sunset Strip . The restaurant served organic vegetarian food , with such celebrity regulars as John Lennon, Julie Christie and Marlon Brando . Jim Baker had two other successful restaurants on Sunset Strip: the Aware Inn and the Old World. [ 3 ] Despite the claims that he had fourteen different wives, he had only one legal wife, Robin Popper, to whom he was married in 1970. They had a daughter together, Tau, born August 14, 1974. Robin said at the time he was "a dirty old man on a lust trip". [ 4 ] Source Family [ ] Baker left Yogi Bhajan in the late 1960s and created his own philosophy based on Western mystery tradition . Changing his name to Father Yod and Ya Ho Wha, Baker became the patriarch of a commune of young people, who considered him their spiritual father. The group, known as the Source Family, lived together in a Hollywood Hills mansion and was supported by the earnings of the Source Restaurant, which grossed $10,000 a day during its peak popularity. [ 5 ] Some of the doctrines of the Source Family were kept secret; however, they generally adopted a way of life that promoted natural health , organic vegetarian diets, communal living and utopian ideals. Father Yod/Ya Ho Wha had a core communal group of 150 people living in the Hollywood Hills. He had 14 wives and 3 children. Music [ ] See also: Ya Ho Wha 13 Music was an integral part of the Source Family and many members were musicians. Father Yod formed an improvisational psychedelic rock band called Ya Ho Wha 13, with himself as lead singer. In 1973 the band began making limited pressings of their jam sessions , eventually releasing nine albums that were sold at the Source Restaurant for ten dollars each. [ citation needed ] The original recordings have become valuable to collectors of underground music. [ 6 ] Celebrities such as Earth, Wind & Fire would buy Source records out of the back of the restaurant. Other family musicians formed various bands including "Spirit of 76", "Savage Sons of Yahowha" and "Breath". Death [ ] On December 26, 1974, the Source Family sold their restaurant and moved to Hawaii. On August 25, 1975, despite having no previous hang-gliding experience, YaHoWha used a hang glider to leap off a 1,300-foot (400 m) cliff on the eastern shore of Oahu. [ 7 ] He crash-landed on the beach suffering no external injuries, but was unable to move and died nine hours later. [ 7 ] After three days of vigil, YaHoWha was cremated and his ashes put to rest at Lanikai Beach in Hawaii. [ citation needed ] Legacy [ ] In 2006, two Source Family members, Isis Aquarian and Electricity Aquarian, wrote the history of the religious group. [ 7 ] A revised version of the book entitled The Source: The Untold Story of Father Yod, Ya Ho Wa 13 and The Source Family was released in 2007 by Process Media, and included a CD with live Ya Ho Wa 13 performances, radio interviews, and Family recordings. The Source Foundation was set up at www.yahowha.org and released lost family music through Drag City Records, Fathers Morning Meditation Tapes through Global Recording Artist, a comic book, and The Source Family in 2012, co-directed by Jodi Wille and Maria Demopoulous. [ 2 ] Much material was gleaned from the group's official documentarian and one of Father Yod's wives, Isis Aquarian. Her archives provided photos, diary, film, cassette tapes of Yod's morning class, lost music tapes, graphics; along with input interviews of Source family members and people who knew Jim Baker (Father Yod) and / or went to the Source Restaurant. The film premiered in competition at South by Southwest Film Festival 2012 and screened at festivals Silverdocs , Seattle International Film Festival and San Francisco International Film Festival , with special screenings at True/False Festival "Boonedawdle" and Hot Docs Canadian International Documentary Festival "Doc Soup" series. In May 2013, the film was released theatrically, premiering at IFC Center in New York City, where its run was extended for over a month. The film screened in 60 cities and had extended runs in Los Angeles, Portland, San Francisco, and Nashville. It is distributed by Drag City and Gravitas Ventures . The Source Family provides a view of the group through their own archival photos, home movies, audio recordings, and contemporary interviews with members of the family. Serving as a highly personal, insider's guide to the counter-culture movement of the early 70s, the film is inspired by the cult-classic book The Source: The Story of Father Yod, Ya Ho Wa 13, and The Source Family (Process Media), which was written by Isis Aquarian and Electricity Aquarian and edited by director Jodi Wille. The documentary features music by Yo Ha Wa, the band composed of members of the Source Family with Father Yod as lead singer.
